items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-08-23
items.q: Many blacks didn't pick up on Elvis Presley right away. But Elvis Presley was a lover of black people, and he emulated a lot of blacks. ... I don't have any recollection of it, but I read about it in certain professional publications and newspapers, where Elvis Presley got into a jam session with hi

ctx.x: Did that cause the demise of that club? Because I don't think it...

I don't think so. No. No. I don't think it caused the demise of the club. I think things started changing with... You see, Club Desire was down in the Ninth Ward. But you had the Dewdrop, the Robin Hood, and all of these Johnny-come-lately clubs, which were just beginning to hit their stride to develop new entertainment. Then, like I said, you had the Coliseum Arena, which was in the central part of the city. You had the ILA Club, which was in the French Quarter. You had all of these things jumping against…
How do you see the difference? Is there any difference between rhythm and blues and rock and roll? I mean, did you see a difference?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: Rock and roll didn't come along until Elvis Presley started shaking his hips, you see.

ctx.x: All right, well. I'm sorry. Let me ask a question. I had a broader question I was going to get back to WMR. Why do you think, finally, at this point in time, that there is black radio, finally? All right.

All right. You've got to remember. Now, we started talking about the black newspapers. The three black newspapers we had, the Informer Sentinel, La Courier, and Louisiana Wheeler, showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them. See, you didn't have jukeboxes. You had jukeboxes, but they were just beginning to highlight the black intelligentsia and…
But you met a lot of women, huh, Tex?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: And here's where the explosion came. All of a sudden, here comes Elvis Presley. Wow! Boy! But you see, Elvis told the story that he was emulating whites...

ctx.x: Did Vernon ever talk about how he, how did he feel when he was coaching Duke Field? I mean, what was his feeling about having Duke Field?

Well, he, well, you see, he didn't like it, but he was trying to make a point to let people know that blacks were qualified to do just about any damn thing. I think that was a period in time that people like myself, or Ebron Jay, who was known as Ernest the Whip, and Malcolm Laplaz, who is now, Dr. Malcolm Laplaz, who now lives in California. We were trying to prove to the city of New Orleans and the listeners that some of us were college-trained people who could open a new era of communication on these radio…
Well, when you hear that terminology, what does that mean? You heard it in the mid-fifties. You first heard it.
